title: A day in Georgetown
summary: A walkable day of museums, a river boardwalk and lowcountry history
description: How to spend a day in Georgetown, SC: the Rice Museum, the Harborwalk, Kaminski House, boat tours and nearby Hobcaw Barony and Hopsewee Plantation.
intro: Georgetown sits at the southern end of the Grand Strand, about an hour's drive from Myrtle Beach depending on traffic. It is a small port town with a historic district, a river boardwalk and a long rice-growing history. It makes a good counterweight to a beach week, and it is easy to cover on foot.

p: Georgetown was founded in 1729 and is the third oldest town in South Carolina. Rice built its fortunes: by the mid-1800s, about 91 plantations around town grew almost half of the rice produced in the country. The Rice Museum, in the Old Market Building with the Town Clock, tells that story with dioramas, maps and artifacts. It is a good first stop to understand what you are seeing on the rest of the walk.

Start at the Rice Museum and the Harborwalk. The Harborwalk is a boardwalk along the Sampit River behind Front Street that runs from the Kaminski House toward the Town Clock, with restaurants, shops and galleries opening onto it. Kaminski House Museum, a house museum on a bluff above the river, has guided tours. The Georgetown County Museum and the South Carolina Maritime Museum are also nearby, and both are free to enter.

Front Street has the most options for lunch, many of them looking out over the water. Walk a block or two off Front Street afterward to see the historic homes in the old town. Many Front Street shops close on Sundays, so Friday and Saturday are the best days for browsing.

list: Cap'n Rod's Lowcountry Tours for a boat trip on the water that made the town.
Hopsewee Plantation for a look at a rice-era house and the grounds. Check its seasonal schedule.
Hobcaw Barony, a 16,000-acre preserve once owned by Bernard Baruch. It is open only by guided tour, and the main tours need reservations.

p: If you stay late, Ghosts of Georgetown Lantern Tours walk the same streets after dark, and the Strand Theater sometimes has a show. Check schedules, since both change by season.

list: Parking downtown is easy compared to the oceanfront.
Smaller museums keep limited days and hours. Check before you go.
In October, the Georgetown Wooden Boat Show draws the biggest crowd to the waterfront.

sections.h: A short history, so the buildings make sense
p: Georgetown was founded in the early eighteenth century and grew rich on rice and indigo grown on nearby plantations, with a labor system built on the enslaved. After the Civil War the town turned to lumber and later steel and paper. Understanding that history makes the museums and historic homes more meaningful, and several local sites tell the story of enslaved people as well as planters. Take your time with those exhibits.

From Murrells Inlet it is about twenty to thirty minutes down Highway 17. From central Myrtle Beach plan on about an hour, a little more in summer. Downtown is compact and best done on foot. Park near the waterfront and walk, since many of the sites are within a few blocks.

If you have extra time, combine Georgetown with a visit to Hopsewee Plantation, which sits south of town along the North Santee River, or with Hobcaw Barony, a large preserved estate with guided tours. Either adds an outdoor and historical element. Check each site's schedule, since tours and house visits run on set times.
